The paper never mentions stress or accent: a full-text search of the whole manuscript for stress|accent|prominen|metrical|foot|intonat|pitch returns 'accent' only as the diacritic names on p. 8, 'pitch' only in the phonetics-of-depressors discussion (sections 2-3) and one bibliography title (Wright & Shryock 1993), and 'intonation' only in one bibliography title (Lehiste & Peterson 1961); no metrical, foot, prominence or stress term anywhere. Corroborated by Odden's field-methods write-up 'Kotoko after 3 weeks' (same consultant/class; consulted again), section 3 'Prosody', p. 7: 'Vowel length does not appear to be contrastive in the language. However, the language does have distinctive tones. Tonal distinctions are at present not very clear, but there seem to be three tone levels: H, M and L. No contour tones have been observed so far. The phonetic distinction between L and M tones is small, in contrast to M and H which seem to be separated by a larger step. Tonal values should at present be taken to be very tenative. Monosyllabic nouns are rare, but H and L (not M) are attested in monosyllabic nouns.' That file has 0 hits for stress|accent|prominen|pitch.

3891.heavy: A word-final syllable that ends with a consonant (including glottal stop) takes the stress; a word-final open syllable does not. 3893.dq: No stress domain is stated; the only framing sentence is p. 3: "Although the phonology of Jɔ remains to be worked out, enough is known to show that it is similar to other Mande languages. On the surface it has only open syllables." The tone description (p. 9) and the stress mentions (pp. 4-6) concern isolated citation forms and suffixed verb forms from a field word list.
3893.prule: No stress rule. Jɔ is described as a tone language with four level tones T (Top), H (High), M (Mid), L (Low), written acute / vertical accent / macron / grave, plus glides (mostly on long vowels). Stress is never defined, marked in the transcription, or located; 'stressed/unstressed vowel' appears only as an unexplained conditioning environment (pp. 4, 5, 6).
3893.srule: Not mentioned in Carlson 1993, §2 'Some phonological characteristics' (pp. 3-12, incl. §2.3 Tone) read in full; the source gives no word-stress rule at all (four-level tone language), so there is no secondary-stress statement.
3893.quote: p. 9, §2.3 Tone: "There are four tone levels in Jɔ. Although most Mande languages have two tone levels, four-level systems are not unknown, e.g. Sembla, Gban, Tura, Yaure (Dwyer 1989:54; Williamson 1989:27). The four levels are labelled T (Top), H (High), M (Mid), and L (Low) in this paper, and are written as follows: T = acute accent: á; H = vertical accent: a̍; M = macron: ā; L = grave accent: à. Various glides occur on single vowels, though these are rare, most glides occurring on long vowels." p. 3, §2: "Although the phonology of Jɔ remains to be worked out, enough is known to show that i…
3893.idn: Jɔ, self-name jɔwúlú 'Jɔ language' (people jɔ̀tɔ̰́nì [sic? scan/diacritics uncertain] 'Jɔ people'), the group called 'Samogo' by their neighbours in the arrondissement of Loulouni south of Sikasso, Mali; Carlson treats Prost's 1958 'Don' of Téna (Burkina Faso) as 'obviously a variety of the language described in this…
3893.tone: p. 9: four tone levels T/H/M/L plus glides (rare on single vowels, mostly on long vowels); tone triplets and pairs are listed later in §2.3. Stress: Carlson never states that Jɔ has word stress, never defines or marks it, and never locates it. The word 'stressed'/'unstressed' occurs three times as a conditioning environment: [r] medial before an unstressed vowel vs [d] before a stressed vowel (p. 4, mārē 'woman' vs páádòì 'lizard'); clusters kl/kr/bl 'quite likely due to the elision of an unstressed vowel' (p. 5); the suffix -rá drops its [r] 'when it is preceded by a stressed vowel, as is the case when it is added to a monosyllabic verb root' (p. 6). These hint at root/initial (non-final) prominence but no rule is drawn, so none is catalogued. Later sources: Kim 2003 (Mandenkan 38) marks haut/moyen/bas tones only and says nothing on stress or accent (a full-text search of the McPherson 2020 (Mandenkan 63, fn. 1, following Djilla et al. 2004) calls Jowulu a three-tone language; PHOIBLE 1287 (from Carlson) lists four tone levels. Tone-level count therefore differs across sources (4 vs 3), which does not affect the verdict).

3894.qtr: The Judeo-Arabic dialect is distinguished by a very peculiar accent that is hard to define. Is it a tonic (stress) accent, is it timbre, is it a phrase accent? One cannot say. In any case, it is certain that syllables are not accented according to their place in the word, but according to their place in the phrase or phrase-member. Moreover, just as in French, the speaker's feeling leaves him free to accent, according to his affective state, now one syllable, now another in the same word, in the same phrase.
3894.dqtr: In any case, it is certain that syllables are not accented according to their place in the word, but according to their place in the phrase or phrase-member.
3894.dq: En tout cas, il est certain que les syllabes ne sont pas accentuées d'après leur place dans le mot, mais d'après leur place dans la phrase ou le membre de phrase.
3894.prule: No word-level stress rule: the source states it is certain that syllables are not accented by their position in the word but by their position in the phrase or phrase-member; the accent (whose phonetic nature — tonic, timbre or phrasal — the author cannot decide) also shifts freely with the speaker's affective state, 'as in French'.
3894.quote: Le parler judéo-arabe se distingue par un accent très particulier qu'il est difficile de définir. Est-ce un accent tonique, est-ce le timbre, est-ce un accent de phrase ? On ne saurait le dire. En tout cas, il est certain que les syllabes ne sont pas accentuées d'après leur place dans le mot, mais d'après leur place dans la phrase ou le membre de phrase. Par surcroît, tout comme en français, le sentiment du sujet parlant lui laisse la liberté d'accentuer, selon son état affectif, tantôt une syllabe, tantôt l'autre dans le même mot, dans une même phrase.

The accent is 'de nature mélodique' (F0 the discriminating cue in 72/77 items; intensity decisive in only 2), but it is non-contrastive and culminative (one peak per accent group, §34), so this is a predictable pitch-realised word/phrase accent, not lexical tone or lexical pitch accent. 3905.heavy: Not a weight-conditioned rule. Olsen states separately that the major syllable is heavy by template ('major syllables are heavy. Heavy syllables are composed of minimally VX', i.e. long vowel or coda) and the pre-syllable is reduced, but stress placement is stated positionally ('always word-final'), never as a condition on which syllable receives stress; the stressed syllable's heaviness is a consequence of the template, not a trigger.

3905.prule: Fixed final. Word stress always falls on the word-final major syllable of the sesquisyllable (= prosodic word = foot): an optional unstressed, reduced pre-syllable followed by an obligatory stressed, heavy major syllable. Native prosodic words are at most two units long, so the rule reduces to 'stress the last syllable' (monosyllable = degenerate iamb ˈσ, pre-syllable + major syllable = σˈσ, Figure 17, p. 53).

3906.heavy: Not defined by the author. The syllables that take prominence in her templates are those with a long vowel (VV; phonemically a geminate: 1.4.3 'All phonetically long vowels and consonants are treated phonemically as geminates of short vowels and consonants', pp. 79-80). Geminate consonants / closed syllables do not attract prominence (CVCCV pa-ṭṭi, ka-ṭṭi, ba-ṭṭi 2-1; CVVCCV paa-ṭṭi 1-2 by its long vowel; CVVCVC kaa-yam 1-2).
3906.dflt: final syllable in disyllables (C(V)CV pa-ṭi, tu-vi, a-ri; CVCCV pa-ṭṭi, ko-ṭṭi: all 2-1); not stated for longer words (all-short CVCVCV ka-ṭa-la, ka-yu-və and the quadri-/pentasyllabic words are listed without prominence numbers, pp. 90-92)
3906.prule: Word prominence (syllables ranked 1 = most prominent, 2, 3) follows vowel length. Disyllables: a long (VV) initial before a short final takes prominence on the initial (aa-na, ee-nRə, ñaa-ma, paa-ṭṭi, kaa-yam, 1-2); every other disyllable is final-prominent (2-1): short-short (pa-ṭi, tu-vi, pa-ṭṭi), short + long final (e-nnoo, e-ppoo), long + long (aa-roo, aa-ṇoo) and vocatives (caa-kkoo, raa-yoo). Net: rightmost long vowel, else final. Trisyllables: a lone long medial vowel takes prominence (i-tuu-ḷi 3 1 2, i-Raa-ne 2 1 2; ka-too-la, pu-Raa-və, ni-laa-və, ka-ṇṇaa-ṭi, ko-ṭṭaa-ṭi 2 1 3); a long initial with short rest takes it on the initial (caa-ka-RRə, pee-ṭi-ccu, caa-ti-kka, moo-ti-ram 1 2 3); with two long vowels the data split (loo-laa-kkə, uu-ḷaa-nti, kRaa-ppuu-ci 1 2 3 vs aa-nRaa-n 2 1 3). All-short trisyllables (ka-ṭa-la, ka-yu-və) and longer words carry no prominence marks. The length conditioning is never stated in prose: it is read off the CV-template categories (all 'A' templates open with VV; 'B' templates open with (C)V or end in VV). One item (CVCVV ti-loo 1 2, p. 87) sits under category B against its own number, but the same word in the pitch section (p. 82, tiloo pitch 2 4: extra-high on loo) shows the final syllable prominent, so the '1 2' is most likely a typing slip for '2 1'. Indira's own 'Stress' /ˊ/ (1.5.4) is a different thing: an emphasis/vocative feature (high pitch, terminal rise, ultra-long final vowel).

3907.dq: Rise in voice pitch and intensity does not always fall on the stressed syllable, as these are high level phenomena involving intonation at the phrase or clause level. Isolated words can be pronounced with very different pitch and intensity from the same words used in communicative contexts.
3907.dloc: Ch. 2 Phonology, §2.5 'Stress', pp. 28–30: opening paragraph p. 28, Tables 2.10–2.11 (minimal pairs) p. 29, examples (11)–(14) p. 30. Also §3.3.6 '-én/-ón: future patient noun', p. 56, and the <in>...-an nominalization note, pp. 62–63.
3907.prule: Word stress is lexically contrastive (minimal pairs in disyllables, three-way contrasts in trisyllables) and may fall on any syllable of two- and three-syllable words; it is realised as lengthening of the syllable nucleus, not by pitch or intensity.
3907.srule: In words of four or more syllables a secondary stress falls on the second syllable to the left of the (penultimate) primary stress, i.e. two syllables before it: [kà.li.bú.tan] 'earth', [ka.Ɂù.ɡa.lí.ŋɤ̞n] 'self', [kà.pɪt.tú.ʷan] 'seventy'; the trisyllables of Table 2.11 are marked the same way ([pá.Ɂa.ɡì], [kʊ̀l.ti.báɾ]; none with a medial primary).

Kakabe is a language with moraic trochees'; every other 'stress' token in the thesis concerns French/Pular source words of loans (§5.5.5, pp. 402-405), the Pirahã/Russian/English onset-sensitivity analogy for H-separator alignment (§5.5.6.1, p. 409), or intonation theory (Ch. 6). The weight- and onset-sensitive foot parsing of L-toned trisyllables (heavy CVV/CVN closes a foot; otherwise the foot boundary precedes the stronger onset, rule 5.102, p. 408) governs where the separating H tone lands, which a compiler could mistake for a QS stress rule; it is a tone-alignment rule.

tn.quote: As for the basic oppositions, the tonal system of Kakabe is characterized by a three-way contrast: H vs. L vs. Ø. Underlyingly every tone bearing unit is assigned H, L or no tone at all (Ø). But at the end of the tonal derivation every tone bearing unit is linked either to H or L tone. Thus, the tree-way opposition at the lexical level gives a two-way opposition at the end of the phonological derivation ... [p. 364] In Kakabe the tone bearing unit (TBU henceforth) is the mora: ... mono-moraic syllables can have only one tone, but bi-moraic syllables can have two tones.
